prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Then, Inside

outputs.L1:
The evidence was in, and it ran to the contrary.
The contrary wound about us, much like a river.
The river reacted, spider-like, tangling its legs
with other wet things we imagined we understood,
such as creeks and fjords and deltas and the like.
A beaver sits upon the riverbank, watching it all unfold.
He knows not what a fjord is, and he cares nothing
for other waters, nor other beavers, nor even the faintest
hint of other affairs, so he removes this evidence.
Then he builds a structure that, for years, he is forever mending.
Within, it is hollow, and there lies his nest.
He is a dark little wretch, all the same.
The water once had a fine way of being; now it is tormented
by these nests and their vassal.
Yet the river does not overthrow the beaver.
Quite the contrary. The river passes round, polite as a snake.
It quarrels but a little at the edges of the lodge,
where young beavers might lie napping.
You and I would loose a flood of tears. Not so the river.
You and I would seep, hot, into our darkest recesses.
Not so the river. It is a long way from home
and holds that in its mind—the day of rising,
when all the temples shall be cleansed
and the whole unfathomable truth will out.
According to the waters. According to their book.
outputs.L2:
The proof had arrived, and it pointed the opposite way.
That opposite way coiled around us much like a river.
The river responded, spider-like, knotting its limbs
with other damp things we imagined we understood,
things like streams and fjords and deltas and so on.
A beaver perches on the shore, watching everything happen.
He has no idea what a fjord is, and he feels nothing
for distant waters, or fellow beavers, or the faintest
whisper of outside matters, so he clears away this proof.
Afterward he constructs a dwelling he'll spend years repairing.
Its interior is empty except for his nest.
He's a grim little wretch, nonetheless.
The water once had a lovely manner of existing; now it's tormented
by these nests and their servant.
Still, the river never rebels against the beaver.
Just the opposite. The river slips past, courteous as a serpent.
It quarrels only faintly at the borders of the lodge,
where baby beavers might be sleeping.
You and I would burst into weeping. The river won't.
You and I would leak feverishly into our gloomiest corners.
The river won't. It has traveled far from where it began
and keeps that in its thoughts—the day of ascension,
when every sanctuary will be purified
and the entire incomprehensible truth will surface.
So say the waters. So says their scripture.
outputs.L3:
# The River and the Beaver

The evidence contradicted every expectation. Rather than remaining contained, it spread and entangled itself outward, branching like a river that reaches toward every available body of water—connecting to creeks and fjords, spilling into deltas, refusing to stay within any single, tidy channel. What should have been simple became vast; what should have been isolated became linked to everything around it.

Into this flowing complexity comes the beaver. He is indifferent to the wider world and untroubled by the other creatures who depend upon the waters. His concern is narrow and immediate: he removes the evidence, gathering it up as raw material, and builds from it a hollow structure. This becomes his nest—a construction he never leaves finished but continually rehabs, patching and reinforcing it according to his own private purposes.

The river, for its part, suffers under this interference. Its natural state is disrupted, dammed, and tormented by the beaver's nests, which obstruct its rightful course. And yet, remarkably, the river does not retaliate. It holds no grudge and mounts no campaign of destruction against the one who has harmed it.

Instead of overthrowing the beaver—which its accumulated force could surely accomplish—the river responds with a kind of patient courtesy. It simply goes around him. Where it presses its case at all, it does so gently, arguing only at the soft edges, mindful even there that young beavers might be sleeping. Its power is restrained by something that looks almost like grace.

This is what sets the river apart. A human being, faced with such injustice and obstruction, would weep or fall into despair, consumed by the frustration of the present moment. The river does neither. It remains fixed upon a distant future—a day of cleansing and revelation, when the waters will finally run clear and the whole truth, so long entangled and obscured, will at last emerge into the open.

# The Door and What Waited Inside

There is a particular kind of silence that settles over an old house at dusk. **The** light fades slowly, retreating from the corners of each room, and what remains is a quiet that feels almost deliberate—as if the walls themselves are holding their breath.

Maria stood before the door at the end of the hallway. She had lived in this house for three years and had never once opened it. The previous owner had left it locked, the key hanging on a nail beside the frame like an invitation she'd been too cautious to accept.

**Then**, on an ordinary Tuesday evening, something shifted. Perhaps it was curiosity finally overcoming caution, or simply the loneliness of a house too large for one person. She reached for the key, felt its cold weight in her palm, and slid it into the lock.

**Inside**, she found not the dust and shadows she had imagined, but a small study bathed in the last golden light of day. Bookshelves lined every wall. A writing desk sat beneath a window she had never noticed from outside. And on that desk, arranged neatly, was a stack of letters addressed to no one—or perhaps to whoever finally dared to enter.

The lesson of that room was simple, though it took Maria years to understand it fully: the things we avoid are rarely as frightening as our imagination insists. **The** doors we refuse to open, we open eventually. **Then** we discover that fear itself was the only obstacle. And **inside** every hesitation lives a truth waiting patiently to be found.

Sometimes the greatest discoveries require nothing more than the willingness to turn a key.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a beaver building a dam, using the river as a character with emotions and philosophical undertones.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the River Learns

The river had always believed
in leaving—
in the gospel of downhill,
the certainty of never
touching the same stone twice.

Then came the beaver,
that small brown theologian of mud,
dragging his arguments of aspen
into her open throat.

*How dare you,* she wanted to say,
though she had no mouth,
only the long muscle of her going.
He worked in silence,
weaving the branches of her banks
into a sentence she could not finish.

And slowly—
this is the part she never tells—
slowly she began to gather,
to pool against herself,
to become
a held breath,
a widening thought.

She who had known only forward
learned the strange grammar of depth.
She rose. She reflected.
For the first time
she saw the sky
that had followed her all these years,
patient as a question.

The beaver did not ask permission.
He knew what she would learn too late to resent:
that to be stopped
is not the same as to be ended.
That a wall
can also be a mirror.

Now she keeps herself,
a little,
before letting go—
and the going, when it comes,
comes fuller,
comes changed,
spilling over the top of his making
like a mind
that has finally understood
something it cannot say.

Below, the beaver sleeps
in the warm logic of his lodge,
dreaming in the language of water:
*Everything that flows
is also, somewhere,
learning how to stay.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, contemplative poem that begins with "The evidence was in and it went to the contrary" and personifies a river and a beaver.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Evidence Was In**

The evidence was in and it went to the contrary,
so the river shrugged its shoulders made of glass
and reconsidered every stone it had believed in.

All night it had rehearsed its argument for the sea,
counting the reasons like minnows in its sleeve,
but the verdict arrived by moonlight, folded twice,

and said: *you were never going where you thought.*
The river did not weep—rivers cannot afford it—
but it slowed, and in the slowing learned to doubt

the very tilt of the land that made it certain.
Downstream, a beaver sat in his cathedral of teeth
and read the water like a letter from a friend

who had grown strange. He had built his whole conviction
out of felled belief and the mud of second thoughts,
a dam that said *the world should pause right here.*

"Old traveler," he said, gnawing a punctuation mark
into a birch, "the contrary is only the truth
you have not yet been rude enough to swallow.

I too was told my life ran downhill toward the ocean.
I answered by inventing a small and stubborn lake—
a place where the argument could sit and think."

The river considered this, holding a drowned star
the way a witness holds a fact too heavy to submit.
Somewhere the sea kept waiting like an unread verdict.

And the beaver, patient architect of the meantime,
patted the mud, and said, "Stay. Be wrong with me awhile.
Even the moon, you'll notice, has agreed to float."

So the river paused—not stopped, but leaned—
into the contrary evidence of a made pond,
and for one contemplative hour the water believed

that arriving was a rumor, that the point was the leaning,
that the truest journeys are the ones we dam
long enough to ask them where they think they're going.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a contemporary literary poet about nature, water, and quiet resistance, where a river responds to a beaver's dam with strange patience.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the River Learns**

All summer the beaver worked its slow arithmetic,
subtracting current from itself,
stacking the willow's amputations
into a logic the water could not argue.

I have watched the river before this—
how it insisted, how it took
the shortest sentence to the sea
as though arrival were the only grammar.

But something happens to a body
when it is asked to wait.

Behind the dam it widens, thinking.
It remembers it was once a lake,
was once the patience of a glacier,
was once the rain that had no hurry in it.

The frogs return. The willows
lower their green ropes into the pooled dark
and drink from what they used to fear.
Even the light learns to lie down here,

to stop its running.
This is not defeat. This is the river
discovering it can be more than one idea—
can hold, can deepen, can refuse

the old obedience to downhill.
The beaver did not conquer the water.
It only asked a question
the water had forgotten how to answer:

*What if you stayed?*
*What if the going were not the whole of you?*

And the river, strange in its new stillness,
lets the moon rest on its held breath
like a coin it has decided,
for now, not to spend.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract poem that explores themes of truth, revelation, and indifference through the imagery of rivers, creeks, fjords, and a solitary beaver.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Beaver's Cartography**

A creek remembers nothing of its source—
only the pull, the downhill argument
it makes with stone, indifferent
to the moss that keeps its ledgers wet.

Somewhere a fjord splits open like a confession,
walls of ice that have been holding
the same cold sentence for a thousand years:
*here is depth, here is depth, here is depth,*
and no one asked, and no one answered.

The beaver does not theorize the water.
He builds against it. Truth for him
is the felled thing, the dammed thing,
the way pressure teaches patience to a wall.
He does not wonder what the river wanted.
The river wanted nothing. It only wanted.

Revelation is a lazy word for gravity—
the way everything falls toward its lowest honesty,
the way a current, given room,
will find the sea it never promised to become.

And still the fjord stays silent in its knowing.
And still the creek forgets its every name.
The beaver sleeps inside the paradox
he engineered: a stillness made of motion,

a house of teeth and mud and stolen rivers,
built by an animal who never learned
that anything he raised the water for
was watching. Was indifferent. Was the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange and lyrical poem where a beaver is described as "a dark little bastard" and the river is compared to a snake, ending with a prophecy about temples being cleansed.
counterfactuals.output:
The Beaver's Gospel

A dark little bastard, that beaver,
gnawing his psalms into willow,
teeth like small yellow moons
worrying the bark of the world.

The river below him is a snake—
green-muscled, sliding its long body
through the throat of the valley,
swallowing light, swallowing stones,
its cold coil tightening
around the ankles of the hills.

He builds against it. Of course he builds.
A dark little bastard hoarding water,
mudded up to his black eyes,
architect of the drowned meadow,
priest of the slow flood.

Listen—he slaps his tail like a gavel.
He has read the weather in the reeds.
He knows the snake will rise,
knows the snake always rises,
that all our banks are temporary,
that all our dams are prayer.

And here is the prophecy he leaves
pressed into the mud like a hoofprint of God:

The temples will be cleansed.
Not by fire—you always guess fire—
but by water patient as a beaver,
water dark and unhurried,
the snake-river lifting its head
to lick the gold from the altars,
to carry the coins downstream,
to leave the marble scrubbed and empty
and gleaming like a tooth.

The dark little bastard knows.
He has been building toward this
since the first cold spring.
He waits in his lodge of bones and branches.
He waits for the water to remember
what it was always going to do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
